posts.title: YE JIN
posts.text: I am currently a master’s student in Materials Science at TUM with a background in software development. I aim to contribute to the development of complete cures for neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s disease and Alzheimer’s. My research interests include micro/nano-biorobotics and brain modeling, driven by a strong passion for pioneering fundamental therapeutic strategies for brain diseases, supported by my solid foundation in materials science.

posts.title: From Microbots to YOLOv11 - My Internship Journey in Cell Culture & Microgel Counting
posts.text: I started my master’s because I want to contribute to the cure of neurodegenerative diseases like Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s, and I’m planning to apply for a PhD in this field as well. I’m especially fascinated by micro/nano-biorobotics and brain tissue or neural modeling as tools for fundamental brain treatment. That’s why I joined the MBRL lab as an intern - to gain hands-on experience with cell culture and to learn how nanorobots can actually be built. At first, I was more interested in nanoparticles, but while writing my research proposal here, I realized how broad the field of microrobotics actually is: Design Actuation Locomotion Planning Tracking Navigation After analyzing four papers recommended by my professor, I found myself most drawn to Design and Navigation. Eventually, I wrote a proposal focused on “Dopamine-Responsive Aptamer Nanorobots for On-Demand and Targeted Levodopa Delivery in Parkinson’s Disease.” Through this process, I became particularly interested in working with BBB (blood-brain barrier) and CMOS-based microrobots. For example, I’m convinced that within the next decade, microrobots will inevitably evolve into self-controlled systems with built-in CMOS. And with continuous in vivo experiments, I also believe that there will be ways to bypass the BBB’s tight junctions and deliver drugs exactly where they’re needed. Alongside the proposal and learning cell culture (including passaging), I was given a very practical task - something that could actually contribute to the PhD students’ projects in the lab: Count the number of microgels and cells in these images. After refining the task with my supervising PhD student, the rules were set: Overlapping microgels and the cells inside them are not counted. Microgels cut off at the image edge with more than 50% outside are excluded. Cells are counted even if they overlap. Cells outside of any microgel are not counted. The output should be a single Excel file (.xlsx) with two sheets: microgel_id_cell_count – microgel ID and number of cells inside microgel_id_cell_id – microgel ID (duplicates allowed) and IDs of cells inside each microgel Since I had already taken AI classes, my first instinct was: wouldn’t segmentation be more accurate? Especially since there’s already a famous tool called CellPose. And indeed, using CellPose I was able to detect microgels… but then the problems started: The pre-trained model was hard to customize. Performance varied a lot by image - sometimes great, sometimes useless. With images full of microgels, it took over 5 minutes per image. (As a Korean, this was unacceptable, way too slow 😂) Cells inside microgels were barely detected. I even tried a naive approach — count “round” shapes inside microgels - but cells aren’t perfect circles, and overlaps broke the method completely. I also considered cropping each microgel into a separate image and then running CellPose… but just counting the microgels already overloaded the server. I literally had to rotate through 4–5 Google accounts just to keep using TPUs. → Segmentation was out. So I turned to YOLOv11 and object detection. Problem: no dataset. Solution: make one. I hand-labeled 49 images. It took me 8 hours straight Haha The model trained, but of course, with only 49 images, it still missed new variations and unfamiliar image types. Still, YOLO was fast, and with a bit of post-processing rules (and some human correction), it was actually practical. So, I built a website. Upload an image → YOLO model counts microgels and cells Human-in-the-loop → check results, draw or delete boxes if needed Get accurate counts of only the microgels/cells you want Export results directly to Excel Plus: export YOLO training .txt labels → quickly refine datasets for future training In short, I now had a pipeline to get labeling done much faster and generate usable datasets for improving the model. And yes… I built the whole website in a single day. 😎 Here’s my GitHub if you want to try it yourself: Frontend Backend I also deployed the website! It’s a bit slow (since I don’t have any lab funding 😅), but it works pretty well using Hugging Face for the server and Netlify for the frontend: 👉 Live Demo

posts.title: Building a Tiny‑On‑Board Anomaly Detector for ESA Satellites
posts.text: Building a Tiny‑On‑Board Anomaly Detector for ESA SatellitesTL;DR — We’re training a lightweight anomaly detector that can run on edge neuromorphic hardware (Akida). It learns what “normal” looks like from satellite telemetry and flags surprises via forecasting errors—great when labels are scarce and compute is tight. We pair self‑supervised learning (contrastive + masked denoising) with an Akida‑friendly CNN/SNN so it’s both accurate and deployable. Why we did thisSatellite ops live and die by fast anomaly response, but ships and ground stations aren’t always available. The goal: catch anomalies quickly with minimal memory/compute and make it work on Akida for true edge inference. The dataWe’re using the **ESA Anomaly Detection Benchmark (ESA‑ADB)**—multivariate telemetry from real missions meant to raise the baseline for anomaly detection. Events are categorized as anomalies, nominal rare events, and communication gaps; the test split excludes comm gaps so the task is to find anomalies + rare nominal events. Two handy, practical bits as you get started: It’s multivariate time series (many sensors over time), so representation learning matters. A 6‑channel subset (41–46) is a great sandbox before you scale to the full set. There’s also a helpful taxonomy: coarse Class labels (e.g., class_4, class_7, class_11) and finer Subclass. Even if you’re doing binary detection, this structure is gold for diagnostics and a future multi‑class head. How the model learns (without babysitting it)Self‑supervised pretraining is the backbone. We explore: Contrastive ideas (Siamese encoders; positives close, negatives far). CPC (Contrastive Predictive Coding) to use context to predict the future in latent space (think: “understand the pattern, not the noise”). Non‑contrastive tricks (BYOL/SimSiam) with predictors + stop‑gradient to avoid collapse when negatives are scarce. Our working recipe is hybrid SSL: a contrastive loss + masked denoising reconstruction in one training step (ssl_train_step). We like Huber for the reconstruction part—it’s robust to outliers you’ll inevitably see in telemetry. At inference time, we forecast a short horizon and treat |prediction − observation| as the anomaly score—no labels needed if you’ve learned “normal” well. Architecture—tuned for Akida (gotchas included)Design for the hardware first. A few rules we ran into: Asymmetric conv kernels (e.g., 7×1) are not allowed. Use symmetric alternatives (e.g., 7×7). This one bit us until we re‑fit the backbone. Stick to Akida‑friendly ops: ReLU6, MaxPooling, GlobalAveragePooling; keep it simple and conversion‑safe. The head is a small forecasting MLP that reshapes to [horizon, channels]; residuals become the anomaly score. Pro tip: Minimize early channel mixing, focus first on temporal features, then add a light 1×1 conv for channel fusion if needed. Training workflow & small fixes that saved us hours Train mostly on normal segments (y=0) so the model internalizes “healthy” behavior; it becomes sensitive to deviations at test time. Windowing matters. A setup that worked well for us: 1‑hour input → 30‑minute forecast. Metrics/Callbacks: If you’re doing binary detection, compile with AUC and monitor val_auc; don’t monitor val_auroc unless you actually added it—otherwise your best model never saves. For SSL/regression phases, monitor val_loss and drop “accuracy” (it’s meaningless there). Normalization buglet: In estimate_norm_stats_ssl, using x.shape[0] can be None with dynamic batches—switch to tf.shape when tallying. Reproducibility: Keep it containerized (docker build …, docker run …) and use a couple of SLURM one‑liners for queueing and cleanup while iterating. How we’ll judge success Primary: ROC‑AUC & PR‑AUC if labels are available (Anomaly vs Rare Event). Unsupervised: Percentile‑based thresholds over forecasting residuals for early flags. By taxonomy: Report by Class/Subclass to spot blind spots (e.g., strong on class_7, weak on class_9). What surprised us SNN/Akida constraints are real—design with the allowed ops/kernels from day one. Data understanding first: relationships among channels and the time range you choose can make or break you. Right tool, right layers: time‑series structure should drive kernel sizes and mixing strategy. Own every line: black‑box DL is a trap; most issues were fixed in training loops/callbacks, not just models. What’s next Lock in the Akida‑compliant backbone (sym kernels, GAP, ReLU6) and validate on the 6‑channel subset before scaling up. Keep iterating on the hybrid SSL (contrastive + denoising) and time‑series augmentations (masking, noise, time shuffle) to harden robustness. Clean up metrics/checkpoints across phases and start publishing results per Class/Subclass; that’s your roadmap to a multi‑class head later. Further reading from the project notes: ESA‑ADB links and SSL papers (BYOL, SimSiam, SwAV, CPC) are all listed in the original write‑up if you want to dive deeper. Here’s my GitHub if you want to try it yourself: Frontend Backend
